Cape Town's Atlantic Seaboard: Foreign Buyers Hold a Quarter of R11.3bn, and Liquidity Is the Real Risk

2026-08-07 · Updated 2026.11.11 12 min read Scott Huang Property

Cape Town's Atlantic Seaboard moved up a tier in 2025. Seeff's figures put Atlantic Seaboard and City Bowl sales at R11.3 billion, up 26% on 2024, with sales above R20 million rising 61% to R4.2 billion. Volume did not explode; value did. That points to momentum concentrated at the top of the market.

The numbers below differ from the version circulating in Chinese-language coverage. The familiar claim is that a third of this market is bought by foreigners. Using Seeff's full-year 2025 figures, this article corrects that to a quarter (R2.8 billion of R11.3 billion, about 25%), and explains in section four why the two figures are not measuring the same thing. Every amount carries a source and a period, and rand conversions use ZAR/TWD 2.01 as measured on 6 November 2026.

Quick answer: Atlantic Seaboard and City Bowl sales reached R11.3 billion in 2025, up 26% on 2024, with R20 million-plus transactions accounting for R4.2 billion. Foreign buyers spent about R2.8 billion, roughly a quarter. In the first half of 2026 Cape Town recorded 115 home sales above R20 million, 13 of them above R50 million. Liquidity varies enormously: the median apartment in Bantry Bay sold in 9 days, while Clifton's median was 682 days — a spread of more than 70 times in one city.

Our position on Cape Town is explicit. This is a narrow, high-value, low-liquidity market, not one where everything rises regardless of price. Section three gives the appreciation, section five gives the liquidity, section six gives the risks. By the end you should be able to judge whether this price band suits your cash-flow structure.

Why are Atlantic Seaboard property prices the most concentrated in Cape Town?

The Atlantic Seaboard runs between Table Mountain and the Atlantic, covering Clifton, Camps Bay, Fresnaye and Bantry Bay, where prime stock trades above R200,000 per square metre in 2026. The scarcity is geographic rather than regulatory: land is pinched between mountain and ocean, so supply cannot expand.

The Cape Town supply evidence is concrete. Nettleton Road in Clifton has fewer than 30 properties and is now the most expensive street in the country. Pam Golding chief executive Andrew Golding says prices of R100 million to R150 million (about NT$201 million to NT$302 million) are no longer unusual there. On the same road, a buyer paid R157 million for a five-level house in 2025, and a Spanish buyer paid R170 million for two vacant plots.

At city scale, the Africa Wealth Report by Henley & Partners and New World Wealth puts prime Cape Town residential at about US$5,800 per square metre, against about US$1,800 in Sandton, Johannesburg. Cape Town is South Africa's price ceiling, yet still below equivalent stock in Sydney, London or Singapore — which is precisely where international buyers start comparing.

(Source: South African financial media billionaires.africa, 2026-11-03, citing Seeff Property Group, Pam Golding Properties and PropStats data; Henley & Partners and New World Wealth, Africa Wealth Report 2026; rand conversions at ZAR/TWD 2.01 measured 2026-11-06)

Cape Town property market 2026: how many homes sold above R20 million?

Seeff recorded 115 Cape Town home sales above R20 million in the first half of 2026, including 13 above R50 million, based on PropStats data. The longer series shows this is not a spike: 190 such sales in 2025, 144 in 2024, and only 49 in 2019.

In other words, Cape Town transactions above R20 million roughly quadrupled in six years. Two forces drive that. Prices moved up, pushing properties that used to sit below the line over it. And the buyer base changed, with external capital and local upgraders arriving together. Transaction counts alone cannot separate the two, which is why the next section turns to medians and price per square metre.

PeriodSales above R20mVersus 2019Note
Full year 201949BaselineTrough of the previous cycle
Full year 2024144About 2.9xDemand recovered after the 2024 election
Full year 2025190About 3.9xDescribed by Seeff as a record year
H1 2026115 (13 above R50m)—Half a year reaches 61% of 2025

“Stock levels remain tight,” says South Africa's Ross Levin, who runs Seeff's Atlantic Seaboard and City Bowl offices. Pam Golding's agents go further: well-located homes sell within days of listing, and cash deals plus purchases made without viewing are both rising. These are supply-side observations, not expressions of optimism about demand.

(Source: South African media outlet billionaires.africa, 2026-11-03, citing Seeff Property Group and PropStats for the 2026 first-half and historical series; counts are for the whole of Cape Town, not the Atlantic Seaboard alone)

Why have Clifton apartments risen 64% in five years?

Lightstone puts the Clifton sectional-title median at R31.17 million for January to May 2026, up 64.1% from R19 million in 2020. That is about NT$62.65 million at current rates, with transacted prices above R200,000 per square metre.

The figure needs careful reading, because it is the most frequently misused number in this market. First, it is the median for sectional-title apartments, not free-standing houses, and not Cape Town as a whole. Second, it covers January to May only, on a very small sample: the same transaction record shows just five Clifton apartment sales between January and July 2026, worth R154.6 million in total. A median of five sales is a price marker, not a trend.

PeriodSectional median (ZAR)Taiwan dollars (x2.01)Note
2020R19 millionAbout NT$38.19 millionPrevious cycle high
Jan-May 2026R31.17 millionAbout NT$62.65 million+64.1% versus 2020
Jan-Jul 2026 (transactions)5 sales, top R55.38 millionAbout NT$111 million1 Victoria Road, 596 sqm

Cape Town price per square metre explains the character of this market better than the median. Clifton now transacts above R200,000 per square metre (about NT$402,000). In the same transaction record, the V&A Waterfront apartment median is R13.88 million, Camps Bay R13.75 million and Sea Point R4.5 million — Clifton's median is close to seven times Sea Point's. These are not different locations in one market; they are different buyer pools.

(Source: South African property data firm Lightstone, reported by billionaires.africa, 2026-11-03, for the R19 million 2020 figure and the R31.17 million January to May 2026 figure; transaction detail and price per square metre from the cmainfo.co.za Atlantic Seaboard record for January to July 2026, 434 sales totalling R3.25 billion, compiled by campsbayguy.com; conversion at 2.01 measured 2026-11-06)

How much of this market do foreign buyers actually own?

Seeff's full-year 2025 figures show foreign buyers spending about R2.8 billion on the Atlantic Seaboard and City Bowl, a quarter of R11.3 billion in total sales. The gap between that and the widely quoted “one third” comes from different price bands and periods in the Cape Town market, not from arithmetic errors.

Start with what can be sourced. South Africa's Seeff annual figure covers the Atlantic Seaboard plus City Bowl, the full 2025 year, measured by transaction value: international buyers around R2.8 billion, roughly 25%. The “one third” figure normally refers to a narrower band, such as transactions above R20 million, or a different sample period. Within that slice the foreign share really is higher, but it cannot be extended to all sales.

An earlier version of this page used the one-third formulation. It is corrected here to a quarter, using Seeff's full-year 2025 numbers, and this note is kept so the old figure stops circulating.

ItemValue (ZAR)Taiwan dollars (x2.01)Note
Total sales, 2025R11.3 billionAbout NT$22.7 billionUp 26% on 2024
Of which above R20 millionR4.2 billionAbout NT$8.44 billionUp 61% on 2024
Of which foreign buyersAbout R2.8 billionAbout NT$5.63 billionRoughly 25% of the total

Buyer origins are worth recording too: agents report steady demand from Britain, Germany, the Netherlands and France, with rising interest from the United States. The impression that Cape Town's luxury property is bought entirely by foreigners is not supported by the data. Most demand remains South African, led by families relocating from Johannesburg and Pretoria, a group whose entry point starts around R60 million.

(Source: South Africa's Seeff Property Group 2025 annual statistics, reported by billionaires.africa, 2026-11-03, for the R11.3 billion total, +26%, R4.2 billion, +61% and the R2.8 billion quarter share; buyer origins from agent interviews in the same report; conversion at 2.01 measured 2026-11-06)

Which suburbs sell fast, and which do not sell at all?

Across 434 Atlantic Seaboard apartment sales between January and July 2026, the median Bantry Bay unit sold in 9 days while the median Clifton unit took 682 days. That is a liquidity spread of more than 70 times within one city and one period, and it is this market's most underestimated risk.

The Cape Town table below uses the same transaction record for January to July 2026, sectional title only. Buyers assessing a suburb usually look at price and appreciation. Sellers discover, at the moment they need to convert to cash, which kind of liquidity they actually bought.

SuburbSalesMedian price (ZAR)Median days on marketCharacter
Bantry Bay12R8.12 million9 daysTiny stock, fastest sales
Sea Point185R4.5 million54 daysLargest volume, over 40% of apartment sales
Green Point77R4.7 million35 daysMost activity in the R3m-R7m band
Three Anchor Bay21R4.5 million41 daysSea Point pricing, quieter streets
Camps Bay14R13.75 million38 daysScarce stock that still sells quickly
V&A Waterfront37R13.88 million—Where international buyers compare prices
Mouille Point34R5.55 million—Beach Road position drives the price
De Waterkant45R3.8 million569 daysSlowest market; price realistically from day one
Clifton5R31.25 million682 daysVery few buyers worldwide; slow but expensive

In Cape Town, the most useful way to read this table is in reverse. If you are buying, a suburb with 9-day medians means deciding on incomplete information with little room to negotiate. If you are selling, 682 days means the price must be right before listing, because this market corrects through non-completion rather than through telling you to cut. De Waterkant at 569 days and Green Point at 35 days sit in the same table for exactly that reason.

(Source: Cape Town's cmainfo.co.za Atlantic Seaboard residential transfer record for January to July 2026, 434 sectional-title sales worth R3.25 billion, compiled by campsbayguy.com; V&A Waterfront and Mouille Point median days on market were not published, shown as a dash rather than estimated)

Where are the risks in this rally?

The dominant risk in Cape Town luxury property is liquidity, not price: a 682-day median on Clifton apartments means almost no ability to convert to cash on demand. Policy risk and currency risk follow, and none of the three appears in a conversation about whether prices will rise.

Liquidity risk in Cape Town is quantified above, and it reinforces itself. Tight supply holds prices up; held prices keep sellers from cutting; unwillingness to cut lowers transaction volume; and thin volume makes the next valuation harder to benchmark. That structure suits long holders and penalises anyone who may need cash within three years.

Policy risk in Cape Town sits at both the holding and transaction ends. Municipal property rates are set from the valuation roll, and the tax treatment of foreign owners plus remittance rules can change. Such changes rarely move prices immediately, but they move net yields. Our separate article on withholding tax for foreign sellers is required reading before transacting.

Currency risk is especially real for a Taiwan-based buyer. At 2.01 on 6 November 2026, R31.17 million is about NT$62.65 million. If the rand returns to 1.93, the 12 October level, the same asset converts into roughly NT$2.5 million less — the property has not moved, but the Taiwan-dollar return has fallen 4%. The reverse also happens, and that windfall should never be booked as investment performance.

One further variable is easy to miss: part of this demand is internal South African semigration. It is driven by safety, water, power and municipal governance, so it will not reverse within a year; but it also raises local holding costs, which eventually shows up in net rental yields. Our net-return analysis sets out the full calculation of yields, taxes and currency.

(Source: Cape Town days on market and transaction counts from the cmainfo.co.za record for January to July 2026; semigration and governance factors from agent interviews reported by billionaires.africa, 2026-11-03; currency comparison between 2.01 measured 2026-11-06 and 1.93 measured 2026-10-12. Market references only, not investment advice; past performance does not indicate future returns.)

FAQ

Is now the wrong time to buy on the Atlantic Seaboard?

No single number answers that for Cape Town, but three facts frame it. Atlantic Seaboard and City Bowl sales reached R11.3 billion in 2025, up 26%, with R20 million-plus sales up 61%. Cape Town recorded 115 sales above R20 million in the first half of 2026. And the Clifton sectional median rose 64.1% in five years. Momentum is real, but tight supply has also compressed liquidity: Clifton's median apartment took 682 days to sell. The question is not whether prices fall, but whether you can carry 682 days without a sale.

Why do some reports say a third of buyers are foreign, and others a quarter?

Because the price band and period differ. South Africa's Seeff full-year 2025 figure is R11.3 billion in total sales across the Atlantic Seaboard and City Bowl, with foreign buyers at about R2.8 billion, roughly a quarter. The one-third figure usually describes a narrower band such as transactions above R20 million, or a different sample period, where the foreign share genuinely is higher. It cannot be extended to all sales. This page uses the quarter and keeps a correction note.

Is the R31.17 million Clifton figure the Cape Town house price level?

No. It is the Cape Town suburb of Clifton's sectional-title median for January to May 2026, 64.1% above the 2020 figure of R19 million, from Lightstone. It should not be extended to free-standing houses or to Cape Town as a whole; over the same period the Sea Point apartment median was R4.5 million and Camps Bay R13.75 million. The sample is also small: only five Clifton apartment sales were registered between January and July 2026.

Which suburbs trade fastest and slowest?

Across 434 Cape Town apartment sales between January and July 2026, Bantry Bay was fastest at a 9-day median, followed by Green Point at 35 days, Camps Bay at 38, Three Anchor Bay at 41 and Sea Point at 54. The slowest were Clifton at 682 days and De Waterkant at 569. For buyers, fast suburbs mean short decision windows and little negotiating room; for sellers, slow suburbs mean the price has to be right before listing.

What do Cape Town house prices 2026 data show that buyers miss?

Three things specific to Cape Town. A suburb median is not a per-unit price: Sea Point alone spans apartments from about R1.2 million to R20.7 million. Currency matters as much as price: R31.17 million converts to about NT$62.65 million at 2.01, but roughly NT$2.5 million less at 1.93. And days on market is a real cost: buying in a 682-day suburb means the exit, not the entry, sets your flexibility.

Why Handle This Through Crestline Advisory?

The difficulty in Cape Town prime property is rarely seeing the flat. It is knowing whether the price is right and whether the money can leave. In one Atlantic Seaboard, days on market run from 9 to 682, so buying the wrong suburb means buying the wrong liquidity.

The three most common failure points

  • Treating asking prices as transaction prices: in this market the gap is wide, and without suburb-level registered sales there is no way to tell scarce from unsellable.
  • Skipping the exit arithmetic: withholding tax on disposal, remittance declarations and the timing of the exchange rate all eat into the headline gain, with little room to fix it afterwards.
  • Never asking how long the suburb takes to sell: Clifton's median apartment took 682 days and De Waterkant's 569, which is information you need before buying, not after.

Working through our partner Crestline Advisory (on-the-ground execution in South Africa) means these are checked before an offer: the reasonable price band verified against registered suburb sales, title and municipal valuation status confirmed, the remittance and tax route mapped in advance, and transfer and handover tracked locally after the sale.
